title: Waiting for an AI law is a poor compliance strategy
content:encoded:
A bank has an AI system in place to flag suspicious transactions and take the call to freeze accounts. While the workflow has a human sign-off in place, clearing around 400 cases a day has resulted in the approval system becoming a formality. So, when a wrongly-frozen account takes the system to court, the bank becomes unable to prove what the human actually reviewed. This, unfortunately, is no longer a hypothetical scenario.

On July 2, 2026, the Supreme Court of India quashed orders passed by the National Company Law Tribunal and the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal in the Pooja Ramesh Singh v. Jammu and Kashmir Bank Ltd. case. The orders had rested on citations generated by an AI tool and attributed to the Supreme Court itself. This directed the Bar Council of India to constitute a committee to prescribe disciplinary norms for advocates who file AI-generated citations.

This is a business story as much as a legal one. Despite two tribunals and several rounds of proceedings, the parties had to carry the cost of a machine error that no human caught before filing. No AI statute was required to reach that outcome. Ordinary law, applied by judges, did the work.

The regulators are moving faster than the legislature

For most Indian companies, the sharper edge is coming from sectoral regulators rather than from the bench.

In early June this year, the Reserve Bank of India gave banks and other regulated entities until June 30 to submit gap assessments on frontier-AI cyber risk. Instead of having the CISO to file the note, the RBI had asked the board to sign one.

Later, on June 24, the RBI publicly released a draft 'Guidance on Regulatory Principles for Model Risk Management' to establish a comprehensive enterprise-wide model governance framework for the financial sector. Here 'models' extend to third-party models, AI, and machine learning (ML) systems used by commercial banks, small finance banks, payments banks, NBFCs, and other financial institutions. So if a lending decision is influenced by a model licensed from a vendor, the model risk sits on the one putting the AI system to use and not the vendor who built it.

Meanwhile, India's legislative position is still a work-in-progress. On October 8, 2026, Union Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw had assured that the time has come for India to get an AI law. In a first step towards this, the government will be launching a consultation paper on regulating artificial intelligence.

However, any business that is treating a pending law as its compliance milestone has their sequencing backwards. Even when the statute arrives, it can only land on top of existing case laws and sectoral circulars, not in place of them. Regardless of what law comes into place, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act takes full effect on May 13, 2027. Businesses will be held accountable even if the data is being processed by an external vendor as the DPDPA will be applicable wherever an AI system handles personal data.

What does this ask of a business?

Behind all the legal vocabulary, the requirements across all the domains are the same—one needs to show their working.

For any consequential decision made by an AI system, organisations must be able to have the visibility regarding which model produced the output, what data it drew on, whether a retrieval step was involved, who reviewed it before it went out, and whether that record still exists six months later.

Multiple Indian firms have written a policy, appointed a committee, and deployed systems but can still not answer any of the above questions. This is clearly an architecture question before it is a policy-related one. Recording the model version, prompt, retrieved data and human sign-off for every AI decision is only cheap if it is thoughtfully designed for. It can, however, become close to impossible to reconstruct afterwards.

It is important for businesses to question an AI vendor before procuring a model. Does the system record which model version handled each request? Can that record be exported and retained? Where does inference physically happen? What happens to inputs after processing? Where in the workflow is a human required to act? Vendors that cannot answer plainly are transferring risk to the buyer.

Build the record now

There is not much point in waiting for an AI law. AI adoption is already in full swing, and when unprepared, the chain is only waiting to break. In the case of the tribunal matter, that chain broke at the review step. In an RBI-regulated entity, the chain is most likely to break earlier, at provenance, if nobody logged which version of which model scored the application.

The current strategy, albeit unglamorous, is to ensure that the record of every AI-assisted decision made can survive being read aloud. So while the law may still be pending, the question is not. When it does come, the answer will have to exist already.

(The article has been authored by Ramprakash Ramamoorthy, Director - AI Research, Zoho Corporation)

title: Omio founder’s advice to entrepreneurs: Find a problem worth solving and stick with it
content:encoded:
AI has made it easier to build products, but entrepreneurs still need to decide what to build and whether they can stay committed long enough to turn an idea into a sustainable business.

For Naren Shaam, Founder and CEO of ﻿Omio﻿Omio Group, the answer is to solve difficult problems, stay focused, and avoid chasing the next big thing.

Speaking at TechSparks 2026, Shaam spoke about building Omio, which operates across 56 countries, and why Indian entrepreneurs should think globally from the beginning.

“If I were to rebuild Omio today, I would start here because there is so much growth and opportunity in India today. But the principles remain the same. You need to go after really hard problems and focus on solving them for a very long time,” he told YourStory.

Shaam founded Omio after identifying a problem in global transportation: operators had separate systems for trains, buses, and ferries. After moving to Germany, he spent two and a half years working on the supply side before launching the company's first product.

“Building a billion-dollar business is really hard. The stories of companies going from zero to a billion dollars very quickly are rare. Don’t get inspired by the exceptions as for most, it is a daily grind,” he said.

Also Read
Google Cloud’s Gemini voice AI wants to do more than just talk

Think global from day one

Shaam believes entrepreneurs need not wait until they have succeeded in India before expanding overseas. While some businesses cater to local needs, sectors such as education, healthcare, and deeptech offer opportunities across markets.

“If your problem statement is already global, you should start early. We entered 30 countries in our first three or four years, even though people told us to win Germany first. That bet, despite the capital required and the mistakes we had to correct, probably helped make us become the company we are today,” he said.

AI has also made international expansion easier. Shaam recalled that when Omio expanded in Germany, it employed around 30 people to handle translations. That work is now done by AI.

However, lower barriers to entry also make it easier for competitors to copy products. Shaam believes entrepreneurs must therefore be more careful about where they invest their time and resources.

“The onus moves from bias to action to judgement: what should I focus on? Which industry has a bigger moat? What will that moat look like 10 years from now? Starting is easy now but choosing what to pursue and committing to it is the hard part,” he said.

Also Read
Swiggy’s Q2: Net loss drops nearly 16%, revenue rises 36%; What sells? The celebrity or the product?

AI may change distribution, but trust remains important

Shaam said AI agents could change digital commerce, including how people book travel. However, widespread adoption will depend on bringing down costs and finding sustainable business models.

“Consumers need these agents to be very cheap before they penetrate the market. There is a cost barrier and a business-model problem to solve. I see this as a major transformation and not an overnight event,” he explained.

Even as more transactions move to AI agents, Shaam believes businesses will still need to deliver reliable services in the physical world.

“Real life happens outside the internet. If an agent buys something or orders food, people need to trust that it will arrive every single time. Businesses that can solve these operational problems at scale will have something valuable to build on,” he said.

For aspiring founders, his advice was to focus on solving a problem rather than on the appeal of becoming an entrepreneur.

“Find a great problem. Don’t become an entrepreneur simply because you want to be one. This is a journey with long periods of darkness, and you need to be passionate enough about what you’re solving to keep going,” Shaam concluded.

title: D2C brands don't need an AI team to get discovered and grow, says Shopflo
content:encoded:
AI assistants are becoming shopping destinations, but keeping up with them can stretch lean teams.

Shoppers are beginning to turn to AI assistants such as ChatGPT and Claude to discover products, compare options and make buying decisions. For direct-to-consumer (D2C) brands, this raises a new question: how do they stay visible as shopping behaviour changes, without building an in-house AI team?

At TechSparks 2026, Mihir Shah, Chief Business Officer at Shopflo by Pine Labs, presented two ways the company aims to help brands tackle this challenge: agentic commerce, which connects product catalogues to AI-powered discovery and shopping surfaces, and AI agents that help businesses improve growth and operational efficiency.

“You don't need an AI team to figure out growth or efficiency for you. You need Shopflo,” Shah said.

Getting products in front of AI shoppers

Brands have spent years building visibility through search engines, marketplaces, and social media. AI assistants are adding another discovery channel, where shoppers can describe what they need and receive product recommendations.

Shopflo's agentic commerce offering aims to make participating brands' catalogues available across AI-native platforms, including ChatGPT, Claude and other emerging interfaces, said Shah. Through integrations, the company streams product catalogue information to these surfaces, allowing shoppers to discover relevant products and, where supported, proceed towards checkout.

For instance, a shopper looking for festive gifts under Rs 2,000 could discover products from a participating brand through an AI assistant. Shopflo's integration with Pine Labs' payments infrastructure is designed to support transactions through these experiences.

Shah argued that brands will need to look beyond traditional discovery channels as consumer behaviour evolves. However, AI visibility does not replace search engine optimisation (SEO), which continues to contribute to website traffic.

AI agents put growth decisions in context

Discovery is only one part of running a D2C business. Brands must also balance conversion rates, average order value, returns, customer retention and profitability, often using separate tools for each function, said Shah.

Shopflo's Growth Orchestrator, which Shah said was available in beta, aims to bring these decisions together. Brands can define their priorities, whether that means pursuing growth or protecting profitability, and receive recommendations based on their store's performance data.

During the demonstration, Shah showed how the system could identify a drop-off between address entry and payment, suggest a fee-transparency banner and propose an experiment to test whether the change improves conversions.

Brands can review recommendations, set limits and approve experiments before scaling them. They can also decide how much autonomy to give the agents.

“How much or how little to use the agents is under your control,” Shah said.

For D2C businesses working with lean teams, the proposition is less about adopting every new AI tool and more about making existing growth decisions easier to manage. Shopflo's approach combines AI-led discovery with tools that help brands act on their own business goals, while leaving the final decisions in their hands.

title: Too much code, too little shipped: Why AI needs a software factory
content:encoded:
AI can generate code faster than ever, but getting it tested and reviewed and into production is a different challenge.

Engineering teams are increasingly using AI agents to write code, fix bugs, and build features. But faster coding does not necessarily mean faster software delivery.

As code generation accelerates, reviews pile up, testing slows down, and teams struggle to coordinate the growing volume of changes.

At TechSparks 2026, Tushar Mathur, CEO of Forge Code, explored this problem in his session, Anatomy of a software factory. He explained how AI-native engineering organisations can move beyond automating individual coding tasks to building systems that manage the entire software development lifecycle.

“Just because code is becoming easy and faster to generate doesn't mean your overall SDLC becomes faster,” Mathur said.

From coding assistants to software factories

The traditional software development process focused heavily on writing code efficiently. Teams spent time defining requirements, preparing specifications and designing architecture to reduce the effort needed during implementation, he said.

With AI taking over more coding work, the bottlenecks are moving elsewhere.

Mathur described how organisations can end up with large volumes of pull requests awaiting review, longer testing cycles and more bugs than existing regression suites can catch.

Hiring more engineers or running more AI agents is not necessarily the answer. More people can increase coordination costs, while adding agents without effective feedback loops can generate code that overwhelms the systems responsible for reviewing and testing it.

“The reason why this happens is because there's no signal,” Mathur said, explaining why simply connecting automated steps does not create an effective software factory.

An assembly line that learns

Mathur presented Forge Code as a software factory that coordinates AI agents across the development lifecycle. The process begins with triaging requests, creating specifications and implementing features.

Agents then verify changes before they move towards deployment, with human engineers stepping in when decisions or feedback are needed.

The system also monitors production, using the resulting insights to inform future tasks. This creates a feedback loop in which the factory can identify problems, improve its workflows and generate new work from what it learns.

Mathur said Forge Code was running around 100 agents in the background during his presentation, working on features, compatibility and bug detection.

He outlined six principles for an effective software factory: autonomous operation, scalability, cost efficiency, measurability, self-improvement and alignment with business goals.

The last principle is particularly important.

Instead of treating every request as a coding task, the factory should work towards outcomes such as improving customer retention or meeting compliance requirements. Teams can then prioritise features based on the value they deliver.

Engineers become supervisors

In this model, engineers spend less time directing every task and more time monitoring outcomes, reviewing signals and improving the system. Business leaders can also contribute requests and priorities directly, allowing the factory to translate organisational goals into a development backlog.

Writing code faster is great. Shipping better software is the real win.

For engineering teams, the trick is turning AI-powered speed into reliable products, measurable gains and business results.

title: 7 Things emotionally intelligent people do differently
content:encoded:
Emotional intelligence is not about staying calm all the time or knowing exactly what to say in every situation. It is about understanding your emotions, recognising how others feel, and choosing how to respond rather than reacting impulsively.

In everyday life, emotional intelligence can influence how we handle disagreements, build relationships, respond to criticism, and navigate difficult situations. People who develop this skill are often better equipped to communicate clearly, understand different perspectives, and manage their emotions constructively.

The good news is that emotional intelligence is not simply something you are born with. Many of its essential skills can be practised and strengthened over time.

7 Things emotionally intelligent people do differently

1. They pause before reacting

When someone criticises them, disagrees with them, or says something hurtful, emotionally intelligent people try not to respond immediately out of anger.

They understand that an emotional reaction can sometimes make a difficult situation worse. Instead of sending an impulsive message or saying something they might regret, they give themselves time to process what happened.

For example, if a colleague points out a mistake, they may initially feel embarrassed or defensive. Rather than immediately arguing, they consider whether the feedback is useful and how they can respond constructively.

Pausing does not mean ignoring your emotions or pretending that nothing bothers you. It means allowing yourself to feel an emotion without letting it make every decision for you.

The lesson: You cannot always control what you feel, but you can practise choosing how you respond.

2. They try to understand before judging

Emotionally intelligent people recognise that their perspective is not the only possible explanation for a situation.

When someone behaves unexpectedly, they try to understand the circumstances before making assumptions about their intentions.

For instance, if a friend takes hours to reply to a message, it is easy to assume that they are losing interest or deliberately ignoring you. However, they might be dealing with work, family responsibilities, or something they have not shared.

Instead of immediately jumping to conclusions, emotionally intelligent people leave room for other explanations and communicate when clarification is needed.

This does not mean excusing repeated disrespect or ignoring unhealthy behaviour. It means distinguishing between what you know and what you are assuming.

The lesson: Understanding another person's perspective can prevent unnecessary misunderstandings and help you respond more fairly.

3. They can admit when they are wrong

Admitting a mistake is not always easy. It can challenge your pride, make you feel uncomfortable, or force you to reconsider something you strongly believed.

However, emotionally intelligent people understand that being wrong does not make them less valuable.

When they hurt someone, misunderstand a situation, or make a poor decision, they try to acknowledge their role instead of shifting all the blame onto others.

A genuine apology involves more than saying, "I'm sorry you felt that way." It means recognising the impact of your actions, taking responsibility where appropriate, and making an effort to behave differently.

They also understand that an apology does not automatically entitle them to forgiveness. Rebuilding trust often requires consistent actions over time.

The lesson: Taking responsibility for your mistakes is a sign of self-awareness, not weakness.

4. They set boundaries without feeling obligated to explain everything

Emotionally intelligent people understand that being considerate does not mean making themselves available to everyone at all times.

They recognise their limits and communicate them clearly. If they are exhausted, overwhelmed, or unable to take on another responsibility, they can say no without turning the decision into a lengthy justification.

For example, they might tell a friend, "I care about you, but I don't have the energy for a conversation tonight. Can we talk tomorrow?"

This approach respects both their own needs and the other person's feelings.

Healthy boundaries also apply to work, family expectations, personal time, and emotional availability. They help people maintain relationships without constantly ignoring their own well-being.

Setting boundaries does not mean becoming selfish or indifferent. It means understanding that care and availability are not the same thing.

The lesson: You can care about other people without taking responsibility for every expectation they have of you.

5. They listen to understand, not just to reply

In many conversations, people spend more time preparing their responses than listening to what the other person is saying.

Emotionally intelligent people try to avoid this habit. They pay attention to the speaker's words, ask questions when something is unclear, and consider the feelings behind the message.

For example, when a friend talks about a difficult day, they do not immediately offer advice or compare the experience with their own. They might first ask, "Do you want me to help you figure it out, or do you just need someone to listen?"

This simple question can make conversations more supportive because it acknowledges that different people need different kinds of help.

Active listening also involves noticing when your assumptions are influencing your interpretation of what someone says.

The lesson: Sometimes, the most helpful response is not advice but the willingness to listen without rushing to fix everything.

6. They do not depend on everyone's approval

Emotionally intelligent people care about their relationships, but they do not treat universal approval as a requirement for feeling secure.

They understand that people have different expectations, values, and opinions. As a result, not everyone will agree with their choices, and that disagreement does not automatically mean they have done something wrong.

For instance, choosing a different career path, declining an invitation, or expressing an unpopular opinion may disappoint someone. Emotionally intelligent people can consider that person's perspective without automatically abandoning their own judgement.

They remain open to constructive criticism while recognising that criticism is not always accurate or fair.

This balance helps them make decisions based on their values rather than constantly changing themselves to avoid disappointing others.

The lesson: You can value other people's opinions without allowing those opinions to define your self-worth.

7. They recognise that other people's emotions are not always their responsibility

Emotionally intelligent people can show empathy without assuming they must fix every uncomfortable feeling another person experiences.

They understand the difference between supporting someone and taking complete responsibility for that person's emotional state.

For example, if they respectfully decline a request and the other person becomes disappointed, they can acknowledge that disappointment without automatically reversing their decision.

Similarly, if a friend is upset, they can offer support while recognising that they cannot control how the friend processes the situation.

This does not mean ignoring the consequences of their own actions. If they have caused harm, taking responsibility matters. The distinction is between being accountable for your behaviour and trying to manage every emotion someone else feels.

Learning this difference can make relationships healthier and reduce the pressure to keep everyone happy.

The lesson: Empathy means caring about how others feel, not believing you must control how they feel.

Final thoughts

Emotional intelligence is often reflected in small, everyday decisions: pausing before responding, listening without interrupting, admitting mistakes, and setting boundaries respectfully.

These behaviours do not mean emotionally intelligent people never feel jealous, angry, insecure, or overwhelmed. They experience difficult emotions like everyone else. The difference is that they can gradually learn to recognise those emotions and respond to them more thoughtfully.

You do not have to master all seven habits at once. Start by noticing one situation in which you tend to react impulsively, seek approval, or struggle to express your needs.

With practice, greater self-awareness and more thoughtful communication can help you build healthier relationships with both yourself and the people around you.

title: Beyond AI: Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026 to spotlight new technologies, markets and opportunities
content:encoded:
For technology entrepreneurs, staying ahead increasingly means looking beyond their immediate business environment. New technologies are emerging rapidly, industries are converging, and opportunities for partnerships, investment, and market expansion are often found at the intersection of different ecosystems.

This makes technology-focused platforms that bring together businesses, innovators, investors, researchers and global technology communities particularly valuable. Bengaluru Tech Summit (BTS) 2026, taking place from November 17–19 at Bangalore International Exhibition Centre, is one such platform worth keeping on the radar.

The 29th edition of BTS will bring together tech companies, startups, investors, R&D institutions, and global technology ecosystems across a wide range of sectors. The participation of global technology giants, Indian conglomerates, unicorns, and soonicorns creates an environment where entrepreneurs can gain a broader understanding of where their industries are headed while identifying potential business connections.

The convergence of the global tech ecosystem

The international dimension is equally significant. Technology communities from 75+ countries, including Sweden, Italy, Australia, Poland, USA, Israel, Spain, Japan, China, Germany and South Korea, will participate across the expo, conference and special events.

This creates an opportunity to engage with ecosystems beyond India for businesses or startups looking to understand international markets, explore collaborations, or simply broaden their technology network.

The grand co-location of embedded world India, organised by Nuernberg Messe India, brings embedded technologies into sharper focus at BTS 2026. With embedded systems increasingly underpinning applications across electronics, automotive, industrial technology and connected devices, its presence adds another important dimension to the technology landscape represented at the summit.

AI and robotics will take centre stage at BTS 2026 with the AI & Robotics Pavilion, led by Bharat fi.AI, spotlighting emerging innovations and advancements shaping the future of these transformative technologies.

Future makers in focus

For startups and emerging businesses, BTS 2026 offers opportunities that go well beyond the exhibition ﬂoor. Through workshops, masterclasses, mentoring sessions, pitching opportunities and product launches, entrepreneurs can gain practical insights, showcase their innovations, connect with potential investors, and explore new business opportunities.

The Future Makers Conclave further brings together founders, investors, and industry leaders, creating a platform for meaningful conversations around innovation, funding, and scaling businesses. Together, these initiatives aim to help entrepreneurs expand their networks, gain visibility, and build connections that can accelerate their growth.

Focus areas at BTS 2026

The breadth of sectors represented is another reason the summit stands out. From IT & deeptech, frontier tech, fintech, health & biotech to electro-semicon, cybersecurity, data centers and Global Capability Centres (GCCs), the summit explores technologies transforming businesses and creating new avenues for growth. It also looks beyond conventional technology domains to emerging opportunities in electric mobility, circular economy, orange economy, and edtech, highlighting how innovation is reshaping industries, opening new markets, and creating possibilities for entrepreneurs.

For businesses looking to identify emerging trends, explore cross-sector opportunities and understand where the next wave of growth may come from, this diversity makes BTS 2026 a valuable platform for discovery, collaboration, and business development.

The future belongs to entrepreneurs willing to imagine, innovate, and take the next step. Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026 is an opportunity to exchange ideas, discover fresh perspectives, and forge connections that can open new doors. Because sometimes, a single conversation, a new perspective or an unexpected connection can be the beginning of something extraordinary.

title: How Stelcore helps brands go global without building everything from scratch
content:encoded:
Selling internationally can open new markets for a brand. But behind every order lies a web of logistics, payments, product certifications, customs rules, and local compliance requirements. As businesses expand, managing these moving parts across countries can become a challenge of its own.

This is where Stelcore Group steps in.

At TechSparks 2026, Founder and Chairman Bharat Mandot explained how the company connects trade infrastructure, compliance, and technology to help brands navigate global markets.

One integration for multiple markets

“Stelcore is about trade infrastructure, compliance infrastructure, and technology for global markets,” Mandot said, describing how the company supports brands entering international markets.

Stelcore says it has worked with more than 30,000 brands and sellers from India over 14 years of operations. It has a presence in more than 14 countries, including the US, Canada, the UK, Europe, the UAE, Singapore, Australia and South Korea.

Rather than requiring brands to establish a separate entity in every destination market, Stelcore brings together importing, storage, payments, last-mile delivery and returns.

When an order arrives through a marketplace or a brand’s direct-to-consumer (D2C) store, the system coordinates warehouse allocation and delivery. Stelcore’s local entity can act as the seller of record and importer, handling applicable compliance and logistics requirements.

Mandot described the model as a way to give brands international reach through one operating partner, without having to rebuild the process for every new market.

Compliance before the shipment moves

Cross-border commerce involves more than getting products from one warehouse to another. Brands must also meet destination-market requirements for product registration, packaging, labelling, certifications and technical documentation.

Mandot demonstrated Stelcore’s compliance assessment tool, which allows sellers to select a destination country and product category to identify relevant tests, reports, import procedures and certifications.

“The tool is free of cost,” he said, explaining that sellers can assess requirements for a product category across different countries in 10 to 15 minutes.

The platform also provides a central repository for product information, including HSN codes and other market-specific details. This can help brands respond to queries from logistics providers and customs authorities, reducing the risk of shipments being held up over documentation.

Mandot distinguished between business and product compliance. While businesses can choose different arrangements, such as working with a distributor or a local entity, product compliance remains necessary regardless of the operating model.

Connecting the entire order journey

Stelcore’s technology brings order processing, warehouse allocation, and last-mile delivery into one view. Brands can access this information through an application programming interface (API) and build their own management systems around it.

The platform also supports services such as tax registration, VAT, customs procedures, intellectual property support, and payment reconciliation.

For brands entering unfamiliar markets, the challenge is not simply finding customers. It is building the operational infrastructure to serve them consistently. Stelcore’s approach is to connect these moving parts through one operating partner, helping businesses expand internationally without having to assemble every layer themselves.

title: AI that speaks, codes and takes action: Inside Google Cloud’s Gemini masterclass
content:encoded:
Imagine handing AI 80,000 files and getting back a presentation with charts, images and a clear narrative. Or asking it to build a detailed 3D scene using code, without dedicated rendering software. These are examples of AI moving beyond answering prompts to taking on complex tasks.

At TechSparks 2026, Rajesh Shivani, Head of AI Customer Engineering for Digital Natives, Startups and ITES at Google Cloud, demonstrated how Gemini is being used across voice AI, autonomous agents and software development.

His masterclass explored how businesses can move from using AI for answers to delegating work to it.

From chatbots to autonomous coworkers

AI tools initially gained traction through chat interfaces that answered questions. The next stage is agentic AI, where systems can plan tasks, access information, and use tools to act on a user’s behalf.

“An agent is nothing now but a model plus a harness,” Rajesh said, describing the infrastructure around a model that manages memory, context, permissions and task execution.

Building useful agents requires four elements: a goal, clear instructions, relevant knowledge and tools to act on that knowledge. A company’s internal data is particularly important because general-purpose models may not have access to its specific processes or customer information.

Shivani also discussed Google’s Open Knowledge Format (OKF), which aims to give organisations a structured way to make information accessible to AI agents.

Voice AI takes on real-world tasks

Voice was one of the key demonstrations. A system developed for Singapore-based Grab helped passengers and drivers coordinate airport pickups despite language barriers. The demo highlighted how voice AI could support interactions across more than 85 languages.

Another example showed AI dubbing an English video into Marathi and Malayalam while matching lip movements and facial expressions. Such capabilities could help businesses produce multilingual training material, marketing videos and customer communications with fewer production steps.

“Voice is becoming the new user interface,” Rajesh Shivani stated, pointing to the growing role of voice-based interactions for customers and employees.

He also showcased a virtual banking assistant created for Citibank’s retail banking experience. In the demonstration, the AI avatar explained options for a maturing certificate of deposit and submitted a renewal after the customer selected a 12-month term.

AI that builds, checks and creates

Beyond voice, Shivani highlighted Google’s tools for coding and cybersecurity. Antigravity helps developers build applications, while CodeMender can identify code vulnerabilities, generate patches and test them in a sandbox.

In one demonstration, Gemini analysed 80,000 files from NASA’s open archives, including Mars weather readings and helicopter telemetry, and produced a presentation using a supplied template and design guidelines.

Another demo showed a model generating a detailed 3D library scene using Python and NumPy, without dedicated rendering software or external assets.

For businesses weighing the cost of AI adoption, Shivani stressed that the most powerful model is not always necessary. “You don’t need to have a frontier model for everything,” he said, explaining why simpler tasks can use faster, lower-cost models.

Preparing businesses for AI agents

As agents take on more work, businesses will need to rethink how their systems handle permissions, security, costs and automated activity. Shivani urged organisations to consider a future in which agents, not just people, interact with their systems.

Developers, he suggested, could increasingly become managers of agents rather than handling every step themselves.

The challenge is no longer simply choosing a capable AI model. It is giving agents the right knowledge and tools, while ensuring they can complete tasks reliably and safely.

title: Lighthouse Communities Foundation lists on BSE’s Social Stock Exchange to scale youth livelihoods
content:encoded:
For many young people, finding a job begins long before they enter a classroom. Understanding their strengths, identifying career options and building the confidence to pursue them can be just as important as acquiring skills.

Lighthouse Communities Foundation (LCF), a non-profit working to improve livelihood opportunities for underserved youth, has marked its listing on the Bombay Stock Exchange’s (BSE) Social Stock Exchange (SSE). The listing follows a public issue of Zero Coupon Zero Principal (ZCZP) instruments held from September 30 to October 14, 2026.

The foundation marked the milestone with a bell-ringing ceremony at BSE on October 29, attended by government officials, corporate partners, philanthropic organisations and its leadership.

A new route to fund social impact

The listing gives Lighthouse Communities Foundation access to a regulated platform through which corporates, corporate social responsibility (CSR) partners and impact-focused supporters can fund its work.

ZCZP instruments differ from conventional investments. They pay no interest and return no principal, meaning subscribers contribute towards defined social outcomes rather than receiving financial returns. The platform also requires organisations to report how funds are used and the progress achieved.

“Models that combine career guidance, skilling and employer linkages, supported by transparent funding, are exactly what our youth need to find stable livelihoods,” said Manisha Verma, IAS, Additional Chief Secretary, Skills, Employment, Entrepreneurship and Innovation Department, Government of Maharashtra, who attended the ceremony as chief guest.

The listing comes as LCF looks to expand a model that combines government infrastructure and corporate support to deliver livelihood programmes.

Helping young people find the right career path

LCF’s Lighthouse programme begins by helping participants understand their aspirations and strengths before they choose a vocational training pathway. The foundation works with partner organisations offering courses aligned with available employment opportunities.

Since its establishment in 2015, LCF has reached more than 2.9 lakh young people across six states. Its Lighthouse programme operates 51 centres, with women accounting for nearly 60% of enrolments. According to the foundation, 77% of placed youth remain employed a year after placement.

The model brings together state and local governments, which provide infrastructure, and corporate partners, which fund operations and implementation.

Dr Ganesh Natarajan, Co-Founder and Chairman of LCF, said the listing was an important milestone in the organisation’s work with underserved youth.

“Ringing the bell at BSE today is a proud moment for everyone who has been part of the Lighthouse journey, from our young people and partner organisations to the corporates and governments who backed us early,” he said.

He added that LCF aims to reach one million young people nationally, helping them choose and build the careers they aspire to.

Pune is the next focus for expansion

The proceeds from the issue will support LCF’s work in Pune, with a target of helping 500 young people develop career awareness, confidence and job-readiness skills to access sustained livelihoods.

In Maharashtra, the foundation works with the Skills, Employment, Entrepreneurship and Innovation Department and the Directorate of Vocational Education and Training under a memorandum of understanding signed in January 2023.

Its initiatives include a Lighthouse centre at ITI Mulund and Model Career Centres in Thane and Nagpur. The partnership has provided career counselling to more than 5,500 young people, skilling to over 2,075 and placement support to more than 3,200.

The next phase is expected to extend the programme to additional Model Career Centres and industrial training institutes, including those in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar and Amravati.

Lighthouse Communities Foundation will report its progress through the Social Stock Exchange’s disclosure framework. For the foundation, the listing creates an opportunity to connect funding with measurable outcomes as it works to expand access to meaningful and sustained livelihoods.

title: Pixxel deepens US push with dedicated federal subsidiary
content:encoded:
Bengaluru-based spacetech startup Pixxel has established Pixxel Federal, a US subsidiary aimed at expanding its business with American civilian, defence and intelligence agencies.

The move reflects the growing role of privately operated satellites in government operations, from national security and resource mapping to environmental monitoring. It also signals Pixxel’s ambition to move beyond supplying specialised satellite imagery towards offering a broader combination of sensing technologies, software, and satellite systems.

The subsidiary will build on the company’s existing engagements with the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) and the National Reconnaissance Office (NRO).

“The US government market represents a significant opportunity for Pixxel as we expand our capabilities beyond hyperspectral imaging into advanced sensing technologies, software, and satellite systems,” said Pixxel's founder and CEO Awais Ahmed, adding that the new unit will enable it to work more closely with federal agencies, understand their mission requirements, and deliver solutions tailored to their needs.

A key part of the company’s offering is hyperspectral imaging, a technology that captures reflected light across hundreds of narrow wavelength bands, including those beyond the visible spectrum. Different materials absorb and reflect light differently, producing identifiable patterns known as spectral signatures. These can help distinguish minerals, vegetation, and other materials in ways that conventional satellite imagery may not.

The US Geological Survey uses hyperspectral surveys to identify minerals, soils and vegetation, illustrating the technology’s potential in resource exploration and environmental research.

Pixxels sees applications in defence and intelligence, including camouflage detection, terrain assessment, and identification of activities of interest. Other potential uses include locating critical minerals and rare earth elements, monitoring crops, and tracking environmental changes.

Allyson Jenkins, who previously led Pixxel’s public-sector business, has been appointed the CEO of Pixxel Federal. The subsidiary’s board includes retired US Army Lieutenant General Ray Palumbo, former Northrop Grumman executive Patrick M. Antkowiak, and former senior intelligence official Frank X. Avila. 

Pixxel also plans to establish an office in the Washington, DC, metropolitan area.

The company’s government relationships have developed over the past two years. In September 2024, Pixxel was selected for NASA’s Commercial SmallSat Data Acquisition Programme, a multi-provider arrangement through which the agency purchases commercial Earth-observation data. In May 2026, the NRO named Pixxel, alongside EarthDaily and ICEYE under its Strategic Commercial Enhancements initiative to expand access to commercial sensing capabilities.

The wider industry is moving in the same direction. US policy has long encouraged government agencies to use commercial remote-sensing capabilities where practical, while retaining national-security safeguards. More recently, the Department of Defense and US Space Force have outlined strategies to integrate commercial space services into national security operations.

title: Hero MotoCorp to increase EV capacity to 80,000 units per month by Q2 FY28
content:encoded:
India's largest two-wheeler maker Hero MotoCorp plans to increase the production capacity of its Vida electric two-wheeler to 45,000 units by March-end and further boost it to 80,000 units by the second quarter of FY28, according to a senior company official.

Hero MotoCorp CEO Harshavardhan Chitale said supply is a constraint, with dealer inventory of just around one day.

"Our dealer inventory continues to be low. We are working with a dealer stock of just about one day, which shows that we are still capacity constrained and there is a strong demand for our product," he said.

The automaker's electric two-wheeler capacity was at 15,000 units per month at the end of the financial year 2026. The capacity currently stands at 30,000 units.

"We have already doubled the capacity. We are well on our way to take it to 45,000 units a month in the fourth quarter. Looking at the demand, we are expanding further, which will take our capacity to over 80,000 units a month by the second quarter of FY28," he said.

The electric two-wheeler market is witnessing strong demand with penetration exceeding 20% in the scooter segment. As per the data from FADA, registration of electric two-wheelers jumped 33% in the Navratri period to 75,758 units, while the total two-wheeler registration fell almost 3% to 8.34 lakh units.

TVS Motor is the market leader, followed by Bajaj Auto, Ather Energy and Hero MotoCorp. All the top four OEMs are ramping up their capacity to meet the surge in demand.

Both TVS and Bajaj are increasing capacity to 80,000 units per month by March, while Ather is targeting around 95,000 units capacity by July-September with its new facility.

"Right now the industry as a whole is definitely capacity constrained. There is far more demand. As and when anyone brings on capacity online and if the product is good, there is an immediate bump up in share," Chitale said.

Hero MotoCorp's capacity ramp comes as the automaker looks to expand its Vida distribution. Currently, it is selling Vida at around 700 of its retail outlets.

"When we put it in the context that we have close to 8,500 points of sale, there is a lot more retail expansion that is going to come to further drive the growth," he added.

title: IG Defence, Oman’s MSA Global explore production of drone systems
content:encoded:
India’s IG Defence and Oman-based MSA Global have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to explore the co-development and local manufacture of drone and counter-drone systems for Oman and the wider Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC).

The agreement links India’s defence-export ambitions with Gulf security concerns, but remains exploratory and does not confirm an order, factory or deployment.

Reuters reported in October that Iran and allied groups had carried out at least 135 drone and missile attacks against 84 infrastructure sites across Gulf Arab states since the United States and Israel began bombing Iran in February.

“The evolving security environment in the Gulf reinforces the importance of strengthening indigenous defence capabilities and developing resilient regional manufacturing ecosystems,” MSA Global chairman Col M. S. Atwal (Retd.) said.

The MoU was exchanged during the India-Oman Defence Industry Cooperation Seminar in Muscat in October. India and Oman already have established defence ties, including joint exercises involving all three branches of India’s armed forces.

IG Defence, formerly known as IG Drones, said discussions will cover three systems. KAL is described by the company as a one-way attack unmanned aerial system with a stated range of up to 1,000 kilometres. BAJ is an unmanned aerial interceptor intended for counter-unmanned aircraft system (C-UAS) use, while JWALA is a micro-missile system under development for counter-drone applications.

“Our partnership with MSA Global reflects our vision of taking India's indigenous defence technologies to global markets through strategic industrial collaboration,” IG Defence Chief Executive Officer Bodhisattwa Sanghapriya said.

The agreement comes as India’s defence exports reached Rs 23,622 crore in the 2024-25 financial year, up 12.04% from the previous year. On October 26, India also approved in principle Rs 2,12,000 crore in military acquisitions, including counter-drone systems and long-range attack drones.

Other companies are responding to similar demand. In May, France’s CS Group won a NATO contract to supply two counter-drone systems for its Brussels headquarters. In August, US firm Powerus announced a separate contract for counter-drone technology to protect Middle Eastern energy infrastructure.

title: Pine Labs Q2 net profit soars 6.5x; Cognizant trims 2026 growth outlook
content:encoded:
Dear Reader, 

The finance ministry expects India’s economy to grow at ​7.3% in FY27.

This estimate, in the ministry’s October economic review, is slightly above the forecast of 7.1% by the Reserve Bank of India, released earlier this month. The ministry has also flagged inflation risks, besides geopolitical tensions, energy price ⁠volatility, ​and tighter global financial ​conditions. But India is “well-positioned” to sustain its growth trajectory, it noted. 

Meanwhile, Zoho’s Sridhar Vembu has a word of caution for all of us: one smart person using AI can do the work of ten. 

“The risk is getting ever more real. This does not mean 90% of people working on a computer will have no work at all… What it does mean is a rebalancing across the economy and that is painful when we go through it,” he wrote on X.

We have to accept this and be prepared, said Vembu, who has spoken candidly in recent times on AI, jobs, and the overall state of the tech industry. At TechSparks, YourStory’s flagship summit, Vembu had said that AI could outperform 90% of coders in six months. 

In other news, private equity firm One Planet Partners has partnered with Japan’s Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Bank to launch a Rs 3,000 crore fund. The fund will focus on high-growth businesses benefiting from India's energy transition, mobility, and manufacturing-led industrial expansion.

In today’s newsletter: 

  • Pine Labs Q2 net profit soars 6.5x
  • Cognizant trims 2026 growth outlook

Here’s your trivia for today: Which tech company once announced a job listing for ‘Pokemon Master’ as part of an April Fools’ joke? (Scroll down for the answer)

Earnings 

Pine Labs Q2 net profit soars 6.5x 

Pine Labs’ net profit rose 6.5 times to Rs 38.6 crore in the second quarter of FY27, while revenue grew 24% year on year to Rs 806 crore. The fintech company had reported a net profit of Rs 6 crore and revenue of Rs 650 crore in the second quarter of the previous fiscal year.

Quarterly highlights: 

  • Pine Labs’ online payments business grew by over 45% year on year, while gross transaction value rose 140%, driven by expansion into agentic commerce, cross-border payments, small and medium businesses, and government segments.
  • According to the company, AI agents now contribute to around 89% of code changes. The company plans to reinvest the resulting efficiency gains in new products, geographies and categories while maintaining a strong EBITDA profile.
  • The fintech firm’s international business spans more than 22 markets. Revenue from Southeast Asia grew by around 40% YoY, while its UAE business crossed one lakh daily transactions. 

Corporate

Cognizant trims 2026 growth outlook

US-headquartered IT services company Cognizant saw its net profit more than double in the third quarter of 2026 while revenue grew by 4.6%. It reported a net profit of $627 million for the third quarter of 2026, compared with $274 million in the same period in 2025, recording a growth of 129%. Revenue was $5.66 billion in Q3 of 2026, compared with $5.41 billion in the year-ago quarter. 

However, the company has trimmed the upper end of its annual growth guidance for 2026. 

Key takeaways: 

  • The financial services segment recorded a YoY growth of 12.3%, while communications, media & technology rose 10.7%. But products and resources saw a marginal dip of 0.8%, and healthcare fell 0.9%.
  • The North America market grew by 5.8%, followed by Europe at 2.2% and the rest of the world at 1.4%.
  • The company has revised its annual revenue growth guidance from 4-5.5% to 4-4.4%, indicating the growth challenges IT services companies continue to face.

News & updates

  • AI acquisition: SaaS major Freshworks has acquired Israel-based AI startup Robusta Dev, an incident intelligence engine that uses AI to investigate tech disruptions, identify root causes, and recommend remediation actions. The acquisition is expected to strengthen the capabilities of Freshservice—Freshworks’ IT service management platform—in incident management and IT operations.
  • Startup incubation: Bengaluru-based AI-powered cybersecurity and threat intelligence company CloudSEK has launched CloudSEK Launchpad, a 12-week incubation programme for early-stage cybersecurity startups. The first cohort will have 10 companies, each eligible for up to $5,000 in AI model credits. 
  • New report: India’s new-age manufacturing sector could benefit significantly from a $3 trillion global AI infrastructure investment cycle, according to a report by Avendus Capital. The investment banking firm says defence and aerospace, space technology, robotics and automation, semiconductors, energy transition, and advanced materials will drive India’s next phase of industrial growth.

Answer: Google

title: India’s new-age manufacturers to benefit from $3 trillion global AI investment cycle: Avendus Capital
content:encoded:
India’s new-age manufacturing sector could benefit significantly from a $3 trillion global AI infrastructure investment cycle, according to a report by Avendus Capital.

The investment banking firm has identified defence and aerospace, space technology, robotics and automation, semiconductors, energy transition, and advanced materials as the sectors poised to drive India’s next phase of industrial growth, offering key opportunities for domestic companies.

The report highlighted 2027–28 as a critical period for commercialisation as companies move from policy support and project approvals towards production.

The opportunity is being driven by rising global investments in AI infrastructure, increasing demand for energy infrastructure, and growing geopolitical security concerns. India’s domestic demand, engineering talent and policy framework could help manufacturers reduce import dependence and build globally competitive capabilities.

“India's new-age manufacturing opportunity is substantial, but its right-to-win manifests in select segments,” said Koushik Bhattacharyya, Managing Director and Head of Industrials Investment Banking at Avendus Capital.

With more than 80% of the $3 trillion AI infrastructure investment yet to be deployed globally, India has an opportunity to capitalise on its domestic demand base, engineering capabilities, and policy support, he said.

Semiconductors and space technology are among the segments showing significant growth potential. India’s semiconductor consumption is projected to more than double from $49.5 billion in 2025 to $106.5 billion by 2030, creating opportunities in chip design, packaging, testing, and specialised materials.

India’s space economy is expected to expand more than threefold, from approximately $13 billion in 2025 to $44 billion by 2033. Domestic defence production is projected to reach around $31.6 billion by 2030, while the robotics market could grow nearly fourfold to $4.6 billion by 2030, supported by wider adoption and import substitution.

The report also expects India’s clean-energy manufacturing ecosystem to move further upstream over the next five years. By the end of the decade, the country could establish an integrated solar manufacturing chain spanning ingots to modules, several gigawatt-hour-scale battery cell plants, and commercial production of indigenous electrolyser stacks and rare-earth-free motor technology.

Advanced materials represent another emerging opportunity, with rising domestic demand and heavy import dependence creating scope for local capacity building. Recycling is expected to scale first, followed by battery materials, while rare-earth magnet manufacturing could advance with policy support.

The coming years will test India’s ability to translate these opportunities into commercially viable manufacturing capabilities, the report said.

title: Startup news and updates: daily roundup (October 30, 2026)
content:encoded:
From Pixxel deepening its US push with a dedicated federal subsidiary to Binance estimating a $6.3 billion impact from a security breach, YourStory brings you today’s headlines with the latest developments across sectors.

Latest news

Binance estimates $6.3B impact from security breach

Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has estimated the total impact of a major security incident at around $6.3 billion, with approximately $3 billion worth of affected digital assets frozen on-chain in coordination with blockchain partners.

In an update issued on October 30, 2026, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange by trading volume said its preliminary investigation suggested that the incident may have originated from a compromised laptop belonging to a DevOps engineer. The attacker allegedly used the access to enter a service container and submit unauthorised withdrawal transactions.

Read more

Pixxel deepens US push with dedicated federal subsidiary

Bengaluru-based spacetech startup Pixxel has established Pixxel Federal, a US subsidiary aimed at expanding its business with American civilian, defence and intelligence agencies.

The move reflects the growing role of privately operated satellites in government operations, from national security and resource mapping to environmental monitoring. It also signals Pixxel’s ambition to move beyond supplying specialised satellite imagery towards offering a broader combination of sensing technologies, software, and satellite systems.

Read more

Other news

Virat Kohli’s stake in Agilitas Sports rises to 6.4% after one8 merger

Virat Kohli’s stake in Agilitas Sports has increased to 6.4% from 1.8% following the NCLT-approved merger of one8 Sports with Agilitas. Kohli had previously invested Rs 40 crore in the company and will continue as one8’s co-founder.

The merger gives one8 access to Agilitas’ capabilities in product development, design, research, manufacturing and retail. The brand plans to expand into new sporting categories and international markets, including the US, UK, Canada and Australia, with the ambition of building a global sportswear business from India.

title: Govt notifies National Social Security Board for gig, platform workers
content:encoded:
The government has notified the National Social Security Board for unorganised workers and gig and platform workers, which will design, monitor, and recommend targeted welfare schemes to bridge the social security gap.

Gig workers are those who perform work or participate in a work arrangement and earn from such activities outside the traditional employer-employee relationship.

Platform workers are those who engage in work through or with online platforms.

In a move towards ensuring comprehensive social security for India's massive informal workforce, the Ministry of Labour & Employment has notified the constitution of the National Social Security Board for Unorganised Workers and Gig & Platform Workers, a ministry statement said.

Established under the statutory framework of the Code on Social Security, this marks a historic shift by integrating digital gig and platform professionals into India's formal welfare architecture, the ministry said.

The Board will be presided over by the Union Minister for Labour & Employment and comprise representatives from the Central and state governments, prominent aggregator companies, employers, civil society organisations, workers' unions, and gig and platform worker associations.

The Board is mandated to design, monitor, and recommend targeted welfare schemes to bridge the social security gap for millions of gig and platform workers, alongside traditional unorganised workers.

The National Social Security Board shall meet at least thrice a year and observe the rules of procedure relating to the transaction of business at its meetings, as prescribed by the Central government.

The National Social Security Board shall recommend to the Central government the framing of suitable schemes for different sections of unorganised workers, gig workers and platform workers.

The board will advise the Central government on such matters arising out of the administration of this Code as may be referred to; It will monitor such social welfare schemes for unorganised workers, gig workers and platform workers administered by the Central government.

It will review the record keeping functions performed at the state level and also review the expenditure from the fund and account.

It will also undertake other functions as are assigned to it by the Central government from time to time.

title: Pine Labs sees 6.5x growth in net profit in Q2 FY27
content:encoded:
Fintech company Pine Labs reported a 6.5x rise in net profit to Rs 38.6 crore in the second quarter of FY27, while revenue grew 24% year-on-year to Rs 806 crore.

The fintech company's net profit stood at Rs 6 crore in the same quarter last fiscal, while revenue was Rs 650 crore.

"Q2 was an all-round quarter - growth across acceptance and issuing, 15% of revenues from global markets, and 14% from products launched only in the last two years," said Amrish Rau, CEO, Pine Labs.

According to Pine Labs, it now processes more than 25 million transactions a day across businesses, up from over 22% on a year-on-year basis.

Pine Labs said its online payments business grew by over 45% year-on-year, while gross transaction value (GTV) rose 140%, driven by expansion into agentic commerce, cross-border payments, small and medium businesses (SMBs), and government segments.

In its international business, which spans more than 22 markets, revenue from Southeast Asia (SEA) grew by around 40% year-on-year, while its UAE business crossed one lakh daily transactions, the company said.

Pine Labs also said AI agents now contribute to around 89% of code changes. The company plans to reinvest the resulting efficiency gains into new products, geographies and categories while maintaining a strong EBITDA profile.

According to Pine Labs it is stepping up brand investments to position itself as the default commerce infrastructure for the global south.

"The opportunity set in front of us is widening, not narrowing," said Rau. "A wider set of new products this quarter, 10 lakh soundboxes committed over the medium term, agentic commerce live on a top Indian marketplace, and a UPI monetisation window opening up — this is the time to build.”

title: Ace Blend bags $9.91M as it looks to scale science-led nutrition
content:encoded:
Ace Blend, a science-led nutrition company, has raised $9.91 million in a Series A2 funding round led by 3one4 Capital, a venture capital firm whose portfolio includes Licious, Darwinbox and Kapiva.

Existing investor Fireside Ventures, an early-stage investor in consumer brands, has increased its backing after leading Ace Blend’s $3.3 million pre-Series A round.

The new funds will support research-led product development and the commercial launch of patented nutrition formats, with the first expected in the fourth quarter of FY27.

Founded in 2018 following more than a decade of research, Ace Blend develops supplements targeting heart health, immunity, sleep, recovery and brain health.

Co-founder Saif Mehkri joined in 2022, bringing nearly three decades of experience in the nutrition industry.

The company said its approach starts with clinical evidence, using research to determine a nutrient’s form, dose and delivery rather than building products around popular ingredients. It also controls sourcing, formulation and manufacturing, while clinical validation and automated testing are conducted by accredited laboratories in Europe.

Partnerships with ingredient suppliers DSM and TCI give it exclusive rights in India to certain technologies, according to the company.

Ace Blend claims 300% growth in FY26, with more than 46% of its customers returning to purchase.

Fireside Ventures principal Ankita Balotia cited repeat purchases and word of mouth as evidence of consumer trust. However, repeat buying alone does not independently establish a supplement’s clinical effectiveness.

3one4 Capital managing partner Pranav Pai said the company was “tackling the hardest problems in nutrition”, including developing formulations suited to Indian needs and maintaining consistent quality.

The funding comes amid wider investment activity in Indian nutrition. TruNativ raised $30 million in June, led by healthcare investment firm OrbiMed. In July, daily supplement brand Supply6 secured Rs 48 crore from Unilever Ventures and Zeropearl VC. More recently, The Stack raised Rs 21.5 crore in October to expand research and its product portfolio.

These investments point to growing investor interest in differentiated formulations, product innovation and repeat demand in a crowded market.

Regulation remains important as brands make increasingly specific health claims. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India has regulations covering health supplements and nutraceuticals, alongside separate rules governing advertising and claims.

In February, the government said there was no dedicated Ministry of Food Processing Industries scheme for nutraceuticals, although broader food-processing programmes support infrastructure development.

Co-founder Saif Mehkri joined in 2022, bringing nearly three decades of experience in the nutrition industry.

title: India needs a digital goods marketplace and control of its distribution layer, say Indus Appstore and Eloelo
content:encoded:
India’s app-first economy still lacks a thriving marketplace for digital goods, and fixing that is as much a question of sovereignty as of technology, according to speakers at the 17th edition of YourStory’s TechSparks.

Speaking on a panel titled “India’s digital economy 2.0: Public tech, AI sovereignty, and the next 500 million”, Priya Narasimhan, Chief Business Officer at Indus Appstore, said the country’s mobile-first habits should have produced a large digital goods market, but have not. She blamed distribution monopolies held by Google and Apple and the economics of their 15% to 30% billing commissions, which make lower-priced digital products unviable. Web stores, the other route, suffer from user friction and low reach, she said.

Narasimhan argued that digital sovereignty is about how and where consumers meet technology. She named three layers India must control: discovery and distribution through app marketplaces, monetisation and billing, and a data trust and consent framework. She pointed to the Epic Games and Google dispute in the US as proof of what happens when developers depend on gatekeepers. She stressed, however, that sovereignty does not mean rebuilding every base layer. The aim, she said, is to plug into global technology on India’s terms.

Sagar Gaonkar, CTO of Eloelo Group, said India’s strengths lie in its data, its cultural variety and its creative and platform-building talent. Chips and large language models can be built upon, he said, with value added for India and then exported. He added that security cannot be an afterthought as more tools are hosted outside the country.

On AI, Gaonkar said it helps microdrama platforms decide what to greenlight before a frame is shot, and personalise what viewers see. He also pointed to stories that adapt to a viewer’s preferences. Narasimhan said app stores must become hybrid platforms: simple and familiar on the surface for most Indians, and addressable by AI agents at the back end, so that developers can scale whether users tap an icon or ask a chatbot.

Both speakers challenged the idea that Bharat is a low-spending audience. Narasimhan recalled that PhonePe’s gold category scaled only after it allowed purchases of Rs 10 a day. Gaonkar said Indian users are value-conscious rather than unwilling to pay, and need a softer landing to experience a product before paying. Narasimhan also urged founders to talk to users rather than rely only on analytics.

Responding to audience questions, Narasimhan said Indus aims to cut the commission burden on developers, and rejected the suggestion that Indians do not value digital goods, citing microdramas, OTT and gaming. She said platforms should not let discovery become purely pay-to-play. On fraudulent installs, she said vetting combines automated checks with human review and constant monitoring, but admitted that no system is foolproof.

title: Binance estimates $6.3B impact from security breach, freezes $3B in crypto assets
content:encoded:
Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has estimated the total impact of a major security incident at around $6.3 billion, with approximately $3 billion worth of affected digital assets frozen on-chain in coordination with blockchain partners.

In an update issued on October 30, 2026, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange by trading volume said its preliminary investigation suggested that the incident may have originated from a compromised laptop belonging to a DevOps engineer. The attacker allegedly used the access to enter a service container and submit unauthorised withdrawal transactions.

Binance said it had found no evidence of any wallet private-key compromise. It added that a detailed technical post-mortem would be published once the investigation was complete and the findings verified.

Binance has temporarily suspended all deposits and withdrawals as a precaution while security checks are underway. It has also revoked authorisation for the affected address and engaged law enforcement agencies and blockchain intelligence firms to trace and recover the funds.

Binance said it would cover all losses arising from the incident through its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) and company funds, assuring customers that their assets remained safe. It also plans to publish an updated Proof of Reserves once remediation is complete.

The incident has prompted a wider industry response, with blockchain partners and digital asset issuers freezing funds linked to the breach. Binance said that approximately $3 billion had been frozen on-chain so far, with recovery efforts continuing.

The exchange said it is working with law enforcement agencies to identify those responsible. The full extent of the breach and the final amount of losses remain subject to investigation.
